test_title: PYST 6: Selection Post (Higher Secondary Level) - GA (Held On 30 Jul, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: gk
question: Which one of the following defines elderly dependency ratio?

options.text: The ratio of children to the working-age population
The ratio of elderly (65+) to the working-age population
The ratio of elderly to children in a population
The ratio of urban to rural elderly population

solution:
The correct answer is __**The ratio of elderly (65+) to the working-age population**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Elderly Dependency Ratio (EDR)** is a demographic measure that represents the number of elderly persons, typically those aged **65 years and above**, per **100** persons of **working age** (defined as those aged **15 to 64 years**). ***Hence, the correct answer is the ratio of elderly (65+) to the working-age population.***

• This ratio is a critical indicator used by **economists** and **policymakers** to determine the potential **socio-economic** support needed for the older population, who are generally considered to be outside the active **labor force**.

• The ratio of children (aged **0 to 14 years**) to the working-age population is known as the **Child Dependency Ratio**, which measures the pressure of the younger dependent population. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• The ratio of the elderly population to the number of children in a given population is called the **Aging Index** or **Elderly-Child Ratio**, which tracks the relative aging of a society. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• Comparing the urban elderly population to the rural elderly population is a measure of **geographical distribution** or **urbanization** trends and does not constitute a dependency ratio. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Total Dependency Ratio** is the sum of the **Child Dependency Ratio** and the **Elderly Dependency Ratio**. It provides an overall assessment of the total number of dependents that the **productive population** must support.

• A rising **Elderly Dependency Ratio** is a common feature of the **Demographic Transition** in developed countries, where **life expectancy** is high and **fertility rates** have declined significantly.

• Countries such as **Japan**, **Italy**, and **Germany** currently exhibit some of the highest elderly dependency ratios in the world, leading to increased fiscal pressure on **pension systems** and **public healthcare**.

• Conversely, many developing nations are currently benefiting from a **Demographic Dividend**, where the **working-age population** is large relative to the dependent population, creating an opportunity for rapid **economic growth**.

• The **United Nations (UN)** and the **World Bank** utilize these ratios to help nations plan for **sustainable development** and to design social safety nets for an aging citizenry.

**Important Points__**

• The **Old-Age Support Ratio** is the numerical inverse of the elderly dependency ratio; it indicates how many individuals of **working age** are available to support a single person aged **65 years or older**.

• In the context of **India**, the elderly population (aged **60 years and above**) is projected to reach nearly **20%** of the total population by the year **2050**, according to the **India Ageing Report 2023**.

• A high dependency ratio can lead to a decrease in **national savings rates**, as a larger portion of the **GDP** is diverted toward the consumption, **social security**, and **geriatric care** of the non-working population.

• To address the challenges of a high ratio, governments may implement reforms such as increasing the **retirement age**, encouraging **private pension schemes**, and investing in **healthcare infrastructure**.

• Demographic data used to calculate these ratios is primarily sourced from national **Census** reports and large-scale surveys like the **National Family Health Survey (NFHS)** in India.
